Marbled flounder (Pseudopleuronectes yokohamae) exhibits a life history closely tied to the thermal conditions of its nursery grounds. Following external fertilisation and a brief pelagic egg stage, the developing embryos rely entirely on their yolk reserves. At a constant water temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C], the time elapsed from fertilisation to the moment of chorion rupture is remarkably short, with the yolk-sac larva emerging approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] after fertilisation. This rapid early development produces a lecithotrophic larva that weighs a mere 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] at emergence, a value that underscores the exceedingly small initial size of the newly hatched individual. The onset of first exogenous feeding follows shortly after yolk resorption, a critical transition that marks the shift from endogenous to external nutrition. The protracted incubation period typical of many pleuronectids is compressed in this species due to the relatively elevated incubation temperature, which accelerates embryogenesis and reduces the duration of the yolk-dependent phase. Field surveys indicate that these early life stages are particularly sensitive to thermal variability.

Sexual maturation in Marbled flounder occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to the species' maximum potential length. The onset of first spawning generally occurs soon after this size is reached, though the precise timing can be modulated by local food availability and temperature regimes. Females at puberty are considerably smaller and lighter than the largest documented individuals. This size at puberty is consistent with an early-maturing strategy, allowing fish to contribute to the next generation before encountering the higher mortality risks associated with larger body sizes. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a predictable allometric trajectory, with the mass at puberty being substantially lower than that reached by fully grown adults.

The maximum size achieved by female Marbled flounder under natural conditions is substantial, reflecting a lengthy growth period following sexual maturation. The ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a dimension that places it among the larger-bodied flatfishes in its coastal habitat. At this maximum size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight for a female is approximately 923 grams [Wwi = approximately 923 grams], a mass that represents a more than eightfold increase over the weight recorded at the onset of puberty. Growth to this asymptotic size is characterised by a gradual deceleration in length increment, a pattern common among iteroparous teleosts that allocate an increasing proportion of available resources to reproductive effort over time. The maximum recorded body mass of 923 grams [Wwi = 923 grams] is derived from empirical length-weight regressions and is consistent with specimen data collected from commercial and research trawls in the species' range. Attaining this size likely requires several years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates.

Reproductive output in Marbled flounder is strongly influenced by female body size and prevailing water temperatures. At 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C], the maximum daily reproduction rate is achieved through the combination of a high fecundity per spawning event and a rapid turnover of clutches. This rate translates into a prodigious annual reproductive output, though in practice most females fall short of this theoretical maximum due to food limitation and the energetic costs of gamete production. Field studies, however, suggest that actual spawning frequency in the wild is lower, as females require periods of somatic recovery between successive batches. The capacity for such rapid serial spawning is a hallmark of many flatfishes.

Longevity in Marbled flounder is modest relative to other pleuronectids of comparable ultimate body size, with a maximum recorded lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] when maintained at a constant temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C]. The species' life span appears to be constrained by the energetic demands of its rapid early growth and high fecundity, a trade-off common among iteroparous teleosts with an early age at first reproduction. The documented age at birth of 10 days [ab = 10 days] after fertilisation at 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C] illustrates just how compressed the earliest phase of the life cycle is, with the remainder of the life span dedicated to growth, maturation, and repeated spawning events. Total length at puberty is reached within the first two to three years, after which growth slows considerably. The combination of early maturation, high fecundity, and a relatively short life span defines a life history strategy geared toward rapid population turnover.
